extracted.intended_audience: Presbyterian ministers, church members, and readers concerned with church polity and the 1689 Revolution settlement
extracted.subtask_description: A presbytery's formal testimony listing grounds to testify against the civil and ecclesiastical constitutions and the settlement of religion effected at the Revolution (anno 1689), arguing they violate Scripture, the covenanted reformation, and the proper order between church and state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil appointment must conform to scripture and covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: The civil constitution called William and Mary in a way 'contrary to the word of God' (Deut. xvii.15; 2 Sam. xxiii.3) by choosing 'a stranger' who were neither brethren by birth nor religious profession, and thus violated the scriptural and covenanted uniformity required for sovereigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders must be 'brethren' and possess covenant qualifications (known integrity, approven fidelity, constant affection, and zeal to the cause and true church of God). Choosing rulers educated in Erastian principles or who take oaths to preserve contradictory religions is a betrayal; such persons cannot be validly set as king and queen of covenanted lands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who participated in prior tyranny/perjury are unfit to choose rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many constituent members of the committee of estates and first parliament had been privy councillors and members of iniquitous parliaments who had framed and prosecuted laws involving murder, perjury, tyranny and oppression, bringing themselves under 'fearful guilt' and forfeiting just right to represent the nation in choosing supreme civil governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons should have given suitable evidence of repentance and received adequate public acknowledgement or censure before being admitted to act as the nation's representatives; failure to purge them vitiates the legitimacy of the settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil constitution failed to re-establish covenanted Presbyterian uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the meeting of estates' claim of right restored more civil liberties than prior tyranny, it did not legally re-establish the former reformed constitution which obliged civil rulers to maintain and defend Presbyterian doctrine, worship, discipline and government as instituted by Christ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper settlement must restore the civil obligation to uphold Presbyterian worship and government; mere ratification of a confession without restoring the full covenanted legal framework is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecclesiastical constitution admitted scandalous and unfaithful members
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution church and assembly consisted largely of ministers and ruling elders who had shamefully complied with public defections, accepted indulgences, subscribed sinful oaths/tests/bonds, or otherwise participated in the apostasy and persecution of former times, yet were admitted without public acknowledgement or adequate censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office-bearers and members who had actively assisted the apostasy or persecution should not be admitted to church privileges or office until purged from scandals and having given evident signs of real repentance (cf. 2 Chron. xxx; Ezek. xliv). The assembly's composition being thus 'packed up' invalidates its moral and spiritual authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolution church is Erastian — civil power encroaches on Christ's headship
rubrics_metrics.description: By acts (e.g., reviving Act 114 James VI, Parl.12th) and practice (king/commissioner present to nominate when assemblies meet; sovereign calling/dissolving assemblies), the civil magistrate assumes authority over church assemblies and even doctrine, thereby invading Christ's crown rights and the church's intrinsic power to meet and judge without dependence on the civil power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The church has intrinsic power, granted by Christ, to convene its courts and determine its affairs (Matth. xvi, xviii). The proper order is ecclesiastical determination first, civil sanction second; any practice allowing the civil magistrate to administer the keys or to assume judgment in matters of doctrine or assembly constitutes Erastianism and is unacceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: State assumption of doctrinal jurisdiction (parliament ratifying Confession) is improper
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament read, voted, and approved the Westminster Confession 'as the public and avowed Confession' in the presence of the estates, without referring to or calling a general assembly, thus assuming the role of judge over doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters of doctrine and the formal adoption of confessions belong to church judicatures; the civil power must not act as the primary adjudicator or approver of doctrinal standards (cf. Confession chap. xxiii sect.3: 'The civil magistrate may not assume to himself the administration of the word or the keys').

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival of retrograde 1592 act shows acceptance of civil control over church
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution parliament revived, renewed and confirmed the 114th Act (James VI, Parl.12th, 1592) in its heads (patronages excepted), an act that prescribes the civil magistrate's authority over the convocation and limitation of church assemblies, thereby perpetuating Erastian encroachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviving an act that makes church assemblies dependent on king's license demonstrates the settlement's Erastian character; a legitimate settlement would not restore statutes contrary to the church's intrinsic authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement is retrograde and fails to revive the advanced reformation (1638–1650)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution settlement left the more advanced reformation attained between 1638 and 1650 'buried under the act rescissory' and reverted the church to a state nearer 1592, thereby disclaiming and abandoning much of the reformation's attainments and covenanted uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A faithful settlement should begin where prior reformation stopped and proceed forward, reviving acts and laws of the reforming parliaments (including measures against prelacy and patronage) rather than rescinding them or leaving them unrevived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to abolish Prelacy in England and Ireland
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of abolishing Prelacy in England and Ireland (as abjured in the Solemn League and Covenant), the Revolution secured and established Episcopacy in those kingdoms, with the sovereign solemnly sworn to maintain that settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper reformation required the legal abolition of Prelacy throughout the three nations; confirming Episcopacy in England and Ireland is a betrayal of the covenanted reformation and a legal bar to their reformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament inverted the scriptural/orderly method of establishing religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than the church acting first in reformation and the state ratifying what the church had done, the Revolution parliament acted first—abolishing/establishing church forms and ratifying confessions—without consulting or hearkening to ecclesiastical assemblies, thereby inverting the proper order of reformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practice and Scripture (examples of Levites, Hezekiah) require the church to take the lead in government and doctrine; the civil magistrate's role is to ratify and defend, not to initiate ecclesiastical constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of ministers who embraced 'toleration' that protected heresy
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ministers petitioned for, accepted, and thanked the duke of York's toleration, which 'extended its protection to every heresy' while excluding field preaching of the pure gospel; those who embraced such toleration were unfit for the Revolution assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ministers who accept toleration that shelters heresy and suppresses faithful preaching betray the gospel and should be excluded from constituting church leadership until they repent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to require public acknowledgment and censure for past apostasy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Revolution managers and assembly admitted many who had, 'contrary to our solemn covenants,' participated in sinful oaths, tests, bonds, or had championed public defections, without demanding public acknowledgments or inflicting adequate censures for their scandals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admission to office or privileges must be contingent on public confession and adequate discipline for those formerly complicit in persecution and apostasy; omission of this undermines church purity and trustworthiness.
